context: Coin change II again provides an unlimited supply of the 3 denominations [1, 2, 5]. Here amt = 5. The goal changes from minimizing the coin count to counting the combinations that make exactly 5. Reordering coins with the same counts of each denomination gives the same combination.
description: A thick gray arrow points right from the coin table at the upper left to a purse labeled “Target amount amt = 5.” The result box below reads “Number of coin combinations: 4.” Four sums appear on separate lines to the right of “Coin combinations.”

The first table below lists the input denominations. The second lists all combinations in the order of the sums shown. Its denomination counts come from counting the coins in those sums. The original figure does not include a separate count table.

frames.explanation: We can verify the count from the input. Using denomination 5 leaves only the single 5 coin. Without it, we can use 2, 1, or 0 coins of denomination 2 and complete the sum with 1, 3, or 5 coins of denomination 1, respectively. These cases cover exactly the four unordered combinations in the table.
frames.title: Number of combinations in coin change II

summary: Using denominations 1, 2, and 5 as often as needed, there are 4 distinct ways to make exactly 5 when order does not matter.
title: Number of combinations in coin change II
